title: To the Parents Driving Home with an Empty Seat
author: Tim Challies
summary: Blogger Tim Challies writes to the parents making the long, quiet drive home after dropping a child off at college for the first time, drawing on his own memory of his wife Aileen's uncontrollable sobbing on the 568-mile drive back from Boyce College in Louisville after leaving their son Nick. He argues the grief of that drive is not really about the physical distance but about the recognition that the family, as it had always existed, has permanently changed -- the child will return, but as someone increasingly formed by other people and places rather than by his parents alone. Challies frames the decision to let a child leave as simultaneously right and painful, describing it as a necessary step away from "the safety nets of home" toward the child becoming "his own man." Having repeated the same drive with two more children since then, he closes by testifying that the grief eases with time and repeated evidence that God continues the formation parents began, and he counsels parents in that moment to entrust their child to God's care rather than their own.
points: Challies locates the pain of the after-drop-off drive not in physical separation but in the recognition that the family as it existed is permanently changed: the child will return, but increasingly formed by other people and places rather than by his parents.

He is explicit that the decision to let a child leave for college is simultaneously right and painful -- "we had done the right thing," and "that didn't make it hurt any less" -- refusing to resolve the tension between conviction and grief.

Having repeated the drive with two more children since his son Nick left, Challies reports the intensity of the grief measurably eased with each repetition as evidence accumulated that his children continued to be cared for and formed well after leaving home.

His closing counsel reframes the parents' task in that moment as active trust rather than passive sadness: entrusting the child to God's ongoing care rather than continuing to feel responsible for outcomes now outside the parents' control.
quotes: We had driven only two or three of the 568 miles between there and here when Aileen began to cry. Actually, she did not merely begin to cry, but to heave great, big, heartbroken sobs. That was the first time I had ever heard her cry so deeply, so fully, and with such an aching soul.
We had done a good thing, of course, and we knew that. We had done the right thing by helping Nick achieve one of the key markers of maturity. But that didn't make it hurt any less.

We knew this marked the beginning of the end of our family as we had always known it. It was not like Nick was leaving the family or seceding from it, but we knew that from this point forward, things would never be the same.

He needed to step away from the safety nets of home, he needed to become his own man, he needed to begin to make his own way through this world. We knew that, and he knew that, though in the moment such knowledge did little to assuage our grief.
He had proven that he would not leave them or forsake them. He had proven that they were his children before they were ours and that his love for them would always far surpass our own.
As the miles roll by, spend a few of them thanking the Lord for his gifts, thanking the Lord for his mercies and expressing your confidence that his plans for your child are only ever good.
